items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Oh when I first moved to New York I started working with Grant Green. Guitarist for Blue Note Records, he played bebop guitar. And he had Bob Cranshaw

ctx.x: When you first arrived it was frightening to you, like did you go to a rehearsal first or did you just land in a gig?
Oh when I first moved to New York I started working with Grant Green. Guitarist for Blue Note Records, he played bebop guitar. And he had Bob Cranshaw, Bob

Cunningham and Ben Dixon on drums and on tour instead he got an organ. Then sometimes we would play gigs with an organ. And then I got gigs with Hank Crawford. Now this was ’63. But meanwhile I would take little gigs with Sun Ra, with John Gilmore playing saxophone. Actually John Gilmore had went with Trane — I mean Art Blakey. He went with Art Blakey. And Sun Ra was using Pharoah but Trane was calling him all the time. John Coltrane was calling him all the time. So there I was, about the same age. So they tried…

items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: My first engagement was with Grant Green and I was working around, and we would tour

ctx.x: I’m fascinated and curious about Sun Ra and I wanted to ask you, you entered that band for however many gigs you did as obviously one of the newcomers and you were sitting next to people like Marshall Allen, who had been there since the get-go. Did you get advice from the band members as well as Sun Ra about how to fit into whatever it is they were doing?

Yes. Yes. I was a young guy at that time. I think I was about 20, 21 years old, and I had just gotten, I had just arrived from Detroit. My first engagement was with Grant Green and I was working around, and we would tour, but on the off weeks I would play with Sun Ra. I was introduced to Sun Ra by a euphonium and trombone player, Kiwami Ziti
